title: The thief who kept the lamp lit
hook: a thief turns up Shiva's lamp on Shivaratri night, and the Rudram's namah bows even to the lord of thieves
carry: namah: the bow leaves no one out
tomorrow: eldest or youngest: whose bow is louder?

segments.voice: Yesterday: shiva is seen by everyone, not only priests, even a cowherd's boy with a stone. Today the week closes with one small word, and a thief.

Gunanidhi was a learned man's son who became a gambler and a thief, and was thrown out of his home. On Shivaratri night, the Shiva Purana says, he crept, starving, into a Shiva temple, where devotees had left food and fallen asleep. The lamp was going out. So he could see to steal, he tore a strip from his cloth, made a new wick and turned the flame up bright. He grabbed the food, someone woke, he ran, and that night he was killed.
screen: `A THIEF ON SHIVARATRI NIGHT.` → `A DYING LAMP, TURNED UP.` → `HE RUNS, AND DIES.`

segments.voice: Then the story turns. Death's messengers come for him, and Shiva's own attendants stop them. Without meaning to, Gunanidhi had fasted, kept awake and kept Shiva's lamp burning on Shivaratri. He's born again as a king who lights lamps in Shiva's temples, and in time, the Purana says, becomes Kubera, the lord of wealth, Shiva's friend. Now listen to the sound the Rudram keeps making. Namo, namah, like a drumbeat. Namah means a bow; it's the word inside namaste. Line after line of the Namakam is built the same way: namah, a name of Rudra, often cha, and. And look who gets the bow. Carpenters and potters. Hunters, and dogs, and the keepers of dogs. And yes, the line says it: a bow to the lord of thieves. The Rudram isn't praising stealing. It's saying there's no corner where Shiva isn't, so there's no one the bow skips. That's a core Hindu teaching, and you can see it in the most ordinary gesture: palms together, a small bow, namaste. Many Hindus explain it as bowing to the divine in the other person. A thief in a dark temple was still close enough to Shiva to turn up his light. So when someone cuts the line, snaps at you, takes what isn't theirs, the hymn doesn't say it's fine. It says they're not outside the bow. Namah. I see you there, and I bow.
screen: `SHIVA'S ATTENDANTS CLAIM HIM.` · `NAMAH: A BOW, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `EVEN THE LORD OF THIEVES.` · `NAMASTE: THE DIVINE IN YOU.` · then, large: `NO ONE OUTSIDE THE BOW.`

segments.voice: Put your palms together at your chest, the gesture of namaste. Bring to mind people from your week, one at a time: someone you love, someone you barely noticed, someone who annoyed you. For each, bow your head a little and say namah, silently. If you pray, end with Om namah shivaya. If you don't, end with the meaning: I see you there, and I bow.
The Rudram. Today's word inside it: namah, a bow, said again and again until no one is left out, not even the lord of thieves.
Your line: namah, the bow leaves no one out. One small word, said again and again. A week walked.

screen: `DAY 1148 COUNTS.` → `A WEEK WALKED.` → `TOMORROW: WHOSE BOW IS LOUDER?`
